g1: Most of what’s been written about communities is way behind on how fast psychedelics have moved from taboo toward regulated use. Oregon’s licensed psilocybin service centers started opening in 2023, and Colorado, which created a regulated natural-medicine system, began licensing in 2025. New Mexico enacted a Medical Psilocybin Act that same year. And since 2023, Australia has given authorized psychiatrists limited access to psilocybin and MDMA for specified conditions.
g2:
They also attract people who love revelation but can’t stand the follow-through. You can meet someone who’s collected 12 ceremonies and 6 origin stories and still can’t apologize to a housemate. Any community organized mainly around the peak experience will eventually learn that the practical work of living together is still there after the insight (somebody has to wash dishes and calm a frightened child).

But in my experience, the case for communal use is real too. Psychedelics can loosen the defenses that otherwise take over every serious conversation. And sitting through a difficult medicine night together can bond people powerfully. Then again, psychedelics can also leave people confused or grandiose. They can leave people dependent, too. And then there’s the mess they can make between people. Is the community around them mature enough to tell the good from the bad?
g3:
Your peers can reality-check the downloads, too. Psychedelics produce convincing nonsense alongside genuine insight, and the two look alike, right down to the lighting. Friends who know your history may notice which parts look like a new understanding. And which parts look like your mother.

And community creates a rhythm. Many traditional medicine systems hold ceremonies on communal timing, not one person’s appetite. With a shared calendar, folks can cut down on compulsive repetition and leave time for integration.
g4: No special shamans, which traditional lineages usually disagree with me on. Many ayahuasca and Bwiti communities believe the medicine should stay under the authority of trained lineage holders. And I’ve learned from those traditions myself. I respect what they’ve preserved.
g5: Even a peer-led medicine culture can end up with an informal shaman (the person everybody trusts and gradually stops questioning, though nobody gave them the title). I don’t know yet how to prevent that. Rotating roles and public accountability might help. And I don’t think either one is a complete fix.
g6: Peer-led never means casual. When authority is spread across a group, people need more competence, not less. So there has to be screening for medical and psychiatric contraindications, plus a review of medications and combinations. You need an appropriate sober sitter. And what calls for professional or emergency care has to be settled before anybody takes anything.
g7:
The medicine stays behind the rest of the pl/ork. Reparenting and somatic capacity come first. So does peer counseling. Medicine can deepen a practice that’s already there. Months of honest relationship, though? You can’t create those by pharmacological decree.

This prerequisite also filters out experience collectors. Someone who won’t spend six months learning to listen without fixing is unlikely to become more relationally mature just because the visions were especially geometric.

Integration is just regular life. The ceremony opens something, and you find out in the weeks after whether anything changed. Any change would show up in relationships and daily behavior. You’d see it in sleep and decisions too. Another sign is whether the person can tolerate frustration without declaring a new spiritual emergency.
